flamboyant

/flam-BOY-unt/ — rhymes with buoyant · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is flamboyant behaves, dresses, or performs in a bold, colorful, and attention-grabbing way.

The skater's flamboyant sequined costume sparkled from every corner of the rink.

Example

A flamboyant performer takes the stage in a glittering jacket that catches the light, towering buckled boots, and hair dyed electric blue, moving with exaggerated gestures to command the crowd's attention.

Flamboyant captures not just 'bold' or 'showy' but a specific blend of personal style, boldness, and attention-grabbing performance—that deliberate, dazzling self-expression is what makes flamboyant more precise than simpler words.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

showy: Showy describes anything designed to attract notice and admiration — a showy trophy case, a showy fountain — and it points at the effect the maker wants from an audience. Flamboyant is more personal: it describes a person whose dress, manner, or performance is bold, colorful, and attention-grabbing as a matter of style.

theatrical: Theatrical means dramatic and exaggerated, as if performing on a stage — pauses, gestures, and voices calculated for an audience. Flamboyant is about bold, colorful style rather than acting: a flamboyant person may simply love loud colors and dazzle without playing any role for anyone.

flashy: Flashy means attention-grabbing in a quick, look-at-me way that often feels cheap — chrome rims, mirrored sunglasses, a glittering signature. Flamboyant grabs attention too, but with confident personal flair: a flamboyant style is bold, colorful self-expression, not just a bid to be noticed.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

reserved: holding back, quiet in manner and style

subdued: toned down, soft, not attention-grabbing

Where it sits · how much attention the style demands — quiet → expressive → bold → flamboyant

quiet vs. flamboyant: Quiet is the opposite pole from flamboyant: a quiet dresser avoids notice, while a flamboyant one demands it.

expressive vs. flamboyant: Expressive is far gentler than flamboyant; an expressive performer shows feeling clearly, but a flamboyant one turns every gesture into a dazzling show.

bold vs. flamboyant: Bold comes close, but flamboyant goes further: a bold outfit makes a statement, while a flamboyant one adds glitter, color, and theater until no one can look away.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — flamboy

Root — flamboy: to flame, blaze (from French flamboyer, 'to blaze,' built on Latin flamma, 'flame')

Suffix — -ant

Suffix — -ant: doing or showing (adjective-forming) (French/Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Flamboy ('to blaze,' from French flamboyer, built on Latin flamma, 'flame') + -ant ('doing or showing') — flamboyant literally means 'flaming': a flamboyant person blazes with bold color and energy, grabbing attention like a flickering fire.

Use the root in a new word: flammable

Use the root in a new word: flammable: The driver reminded everyone that flammable liquids are never allowed on the bus.

Word Choice

neutral / informal

Use flamboyant when someone's personality, style, or performance is deliberately bold, colorful, and attention-grabbing. For just 'showy' or 'visible,' simpler words work better.
